title: Japan legend Miura, 59, scores first goal since 2022
description: Kazuyoshi Miura, the world's oldest professional footballer, scores his first goal in nearly four years at the age of 59 for Japanese third-tier side Fukushima United.
fullText:
Kazuyoshi Miura, the world's oldest professional footballer, scored his first goal in nearly four years at the age of 59 for Japanese third-tier side Fukushima United.

Miura found the net in the 52nd minute to make it 5-0 to Fukushima in an eventual 7-0 win over Iwaki Furukawa in the Emperor's Cup on Saturday.

It is his first competitive goal since netting for Suzuka PG, now Atletico Suzuka, against FC Osaka in November 2022.

Dubbed 'King Kazu' in Japan, he is one of the country's most loved sportsmen and was the face of the J League when it launched in 1993.

He started his career with Brazilian side Santos in 1986 and has also played club football in Italy, Croatia and Australia.

The forward's long career will enter a 42nd season after extending his loan at Fukushima from J2 League side Yokohama FC until June 2027.

title: Pogacar wins fifth Tour title amid Paris finish drama
description: Slovenian Tadej Pogacar wins the Tour de France for a record-equalling fifth time.
fullText:
Slovenian Tadej Pogacar won the Tour de France for a record-equalling fifth time.

The 27-year-old UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider crossed the line on Paris' Champs-Elysees in the peloton, to join Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain as the endurance event's most successful male riders.

All-conquering Pogacar raised the idea that his remarkable reality is proving stranger than fiction, describing it as "something you wouldn't even maybe write in a story book".

The three-week Grand Tour's final stage was won by the Netherlands' Mathieu van der Poel of Alpecin-Premier Tech after a frantic charge to the line on the French capital's famous cobbles in which he pipped team-mate Jasper Philipsen of Belgium by inches.

Pogacar's victory means he is positioned by many as the greatest cyclist of all time, superseding the achievements and status of Belgian legend Merckx.

It also marks Pogacar's third Tour win in succession and includes a record-breaking ascent of the iconic Alpe d'Huez on stage 19, when he sealed another dominant victory.

It was the last of five stage wins in a race in which Pogacar used his explosive launch and unmatchable metronomic pace to see off his rivals, who for some time have had virtually no answer.

Pogacar has won almost every major race in the sport, including the Tour of Flanders, Giro d'Italia, Milan-San Remo, Road World Championships, Giro di Lombardia and Liege-Bastogne-Liege.

Pogacar was booed by some fans during the Tour, as his performances are often so far ahead of any of his peers that some feel frustrated the sport is losing its competitive edge.

He now has 127 wins in an eight-year elite professional career.

"Victory is really special," said Pogacar. "Thank you to all the fans and my team.

"But the biggest thanks goes to all my family who support me all my life. My parents - without them I would not be standing here five times already.

"Seven Tours and seven times on the podium, and five wins, is something you wouldn't even maybe write in a story book, and it's unbelievable for me.

"It's a magnificent podium with some incredible champions to fight with.

"It's a shame Jonas [Vingegaard] crashed out this time and many others. I hope they have a quick recovery and next year we fight again."

The famous final stage, which for the overall contenders is an unchallenged formality, typically becomes a flat bunch sprint.

Last year organisers ASO introduced a circuit which takes on a cobbled climb over the city's famous Montmartre hill, changing the parcours enough to encourage the heavier, more powerful riders to challenge for victory.

On Sunday it was powerhouse classics legend Van der Poel who took victory after charging away with 11km remaining with Pogacar.

Pogacar and Van der Poel led through the picturesque and narrow lanes over Montmartre and past Sacre-Coeur, where some fans had mobile phones knocked out of their hands as the riders squeezed past at speed, before Pogacar began to fade after three weeks of dominance and showing no weakness.

Van der Poel, whose strength and staying power allow him to pull out gaps in gruelling one-day races, just managed to stay ahead of a chasing pack which included several sprinters and was rapidly closing, before he crossed the line, collapsed off his bike and lay under a barrier, breathing heavily for several minutes.

Van der Poel added this prestigious victory on the famous cobbles to many of the sport's biggest one-day races, such as multiple victories in Paris-Roubaix and the Tour of Flanders.

He said: "We have a saying in Dutch that it has to come for your toes. I don't know where this came from, but not from my toes."

The stage was reduced from 133km to 89km after the redirection of emergency services to help tackle wildfires in south-west France.

The one rider who has broken Pogacar's stranglehold of cycling's biggest race in the past was Denmark's Vingegaard, who won in 2022 and 2023.

But this year the 29-year-old Visma-Lease a Bike rider abandoned after breaking his collarbone on a easy right-hand bend on stage 15.

The mistake was very unlike Vingegaard's near perfect technique and execution as a rider, and attention soon turned to scrutiny of the International Testing Agency (ITA), which had awoken Vingegaard at 2am to carry out an anti-doping test.

Other riders had the same treatment, including Pogacar at 5am, but the ITA said there was "exceptional circumstances" to take the night tests, which are rare and require additional permission.

It is not known when the test results will be published.

Pogacar's only other real rival was the much-improved Belgian Remco Evenepoel of Red Bull-Bora-Hansgohe, who finished six minutes 26 seconds behind overall.

Third place went to Pogacar's Mexican team-mate Isaac del Toro, who won stage two thanks largely to Pogacar's babysitting pace in the lead-up to the line.

It would not be the only time Pogacar would aid Del Toro, 22, sacrificing his own potential victory on Saturday's brutal 'queen' stage to Alpe d'Huez to consolidate Del Toro's place on the podium.

Del Toro's white jersey for the best young rider came at the expense of France's new 19-year-old star Paul Seixas of Decathlon-CMA CGM. Seixas looked stronger than Del Toro at times on the climbs but faded substantially on Saturday.

Many think Seixas will be a rival to Pogacar in the future.

In the year when Britain's four-time Tour winner Chris Froome retired, his former team - now known as Netcompany Ineos Cycling - failed to record a stage victory in 21 attempts.

Ex-Ineos rider Tom Pidcock of Pinarello-Q36.5 won on Alpe d'Huez four years ago and returned to this race having achieved much with a new team built entirely around him.

The 26-year-old did not manage to win a stage, but he and his team will be satisfied with Pidcock's consistent battling riding, which earned him ninth in the general classification to build on third place in last year's Vuelta a Espana.

Fellow Briton Adam Yates, 33, showed great tenacity after falling ill on stage 16 and spending two days riding at the back of the field before helping pace Pogacar up a climb for victory on stage 19.

One of the most entertaining riders in the race was Ecuador's Richard Carapaz of EF Education-Easypost. He toiled earlier in the race before coming into great form to claim the king of the mountains' polka dot jersey.

He won stage 18 and Saturday's stage 20 after topping the race's highest point first and after 5,450km of climbing.

The green points jersey was awarded to Denmark's Mads Pedersen of Lidl-Trek, after tenacious riding on climbs he is not typically strong on to hoover up mid-stage points, alongside winning stage four.

He beat a number of sprinters to the jersey, including Philipsen of Alpecin-Premier Tech. Philipsen won stage 17 and fellow Belgian Tim Merlier of Soudal-Quick Step won three bunch sprint stages.

title: Evans steps out of shadows into spotlight with Scotland's fourth gold
description: Angharad Evans was overlooked before these Commonwealth Games. But now the Scotland swimmer is a gold medallist.
fullText:
Angharad Evans was overlooked before these Commonwealth Games.

She wasn't being talked about and that was a mistake, one of her team-mates said. Turns out Duncan Scott knows a bit about swimming...

Scotland's most decorated Games has 14 medals of his own, but Evans now has her first after edging out her rivals in 100m breaststroke.

Amid febrile scenes at Tollcross, the 23-year-old held off Aimee Canny of South Africa down the stretch to earn the hosts' fourth gold in three days.

"Touching the wall, hearing that crowd, then the roar when I was on the podium was just... you can't even dream of moments like that. It was unreal," Evans - clutching a special golden version of Games mascot Finnie - told BBC Sport Scotland.

"I was holding it together until I saw my family and that was just such an emotional moment. It will be with me for the rest of my life.

Gymnast Ward goes from Glasgow dreamer to gold medallist

Scott overcomes pressure and big pal Dean to give Scotland golden start

Why is it so special to be part of Team Scotland?

Given Evans qualified fastest - and fastest by a distance - any pre-Games ignorance had already evaporated by the time she strode out into this clammy, claustrophic cauldron of noise on Sunday.

The Cambridge-born athlete could have represented England or Wales through her parents but, after choosing to train at the University of Stirling upon her return from studying in the United States, she opted for Scotland.

And the noise that greeted her before - and carried her through - her race was rich reward for that decision.

As Evans' impressive nails - adorned with Saltires, the T of a well-known lager brand, Nessie, and the words 'Irn Bru' - sliced through the water, the crowd grew louder and louder, culminating in a huge wave of noise when she touched the wall.

Afterwards, she confessed to wondering during the race why she didn't feel more stressed but also thanks the Scottish fans for helping her during the tickly bit.

"It's not the biggest crowd I've competed in front of, but it's the loudest and the most passionate," added Evans, who was sixth in this event at the Paris Olympics. "I felt their energy and love especially in the last five metres when it hurt.

"I had the choice of England, Wales or Scotland but Scotland felt right, it felt like home. They made me the athlete I am today and I dreamed of getting a gold and having the crowd roar and this is that but 100 times bigger."

Alarmingly for her rivals, Evans' main event is still to come. The 200m on Wednesday was considered pre-meet a more likely medal prospect for her.

So could she find herself revelling in the Tollcross atmosphere once more?

"I don't think you can top how that felt tonight but we'll see how it goes," she said.

title: Norris and McLaren almost perfect as Ferrari flounder in Hungary
description: Lando Norris' first grand prix win of 2026 was a long time coming as the mistakes piled up for Ferrari in Hungary, writes Andrew Benson.
fullText:
Lando Norris ended the first half of the Formula 1 season with a victory in the Hungarian Grand Prix that he described as "one of my best performances".

It was a drive that had been a long time coming, after a difficult start to the season for the reigning world champion and his McLaren team.

But when McLaren finally gave him a car of the performance level he had become used to in the past season and a half, he more than made the most of it.

While Ferrari, the pre-race favourites, floundered and made, in the words of their team boss Frederic Vasseur "too many mistakes", Norris and McLaren were almost perfect.

Even in the context of Kimi Antonelli's stellar start to the season for Mercedes, this was one of the most impressive and convincing victories of the season.

Norris' one mistake was on the first lap. He converted his pole position into a lead at the first corner, only to misjudge the grip available at Turn Two, slide wide, and gift his position to team-mate Oscar Piastri.

It looked to have been a potentially fatal error to his victory hopes on a track where overtaking is all but impossible between evenly matched cars on similar strategies, but Norris stayed calm.

Seeing he could easily keep pace with Piastri despite being in the dirty air, he said he always believed the win was on.

"It wasn't my finest Turn Two," Norris said, "but after that, seeing what my pace was like and I was just better in every sense, in terms of degradation and pace, I was convinced I could still win the race."

Trapped, Norris begged for a different strategy to give himself a chance of victory, and eventually circumstances presented it to him.

Around half-distance. McLaren pitted Piastri to cover off Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari, which had just stopped for fresh tyres. That gave Norris clean air and he set a blistering pace.

Piastri might still have held the lead, but for a collision with Carlos Sainz as he lapped his Williams. The Australian was angry after Norris came out ahead from his stop a few laps later - but at the Spaniard, not McLaren.

"The fact I could keep up with Oscar on this kind of track, where it's impossible to follow and impossible to overtake, I was within 0.8 seconds or something for, I don't know, almost 40 laps, the fact I could do this is what gave me confidence that I'd win the race no matter what, whether he boxed early or late or whatever," Norris said.

"The pace advantage I had was huge today. But I don't know why. The cars are identical, and I've just been feeling very strong lately.

"I've worked on many areas from last year. I feel much more confident lately with how to extract performance, and I've worked a lot with my engineers to understand this car because it's certainly not an easy car to understand and figure out how to drive on the limit consistently.

"So, why? Just hard work. Hard work from my engineers and from myself to improve me as a driver and improve my driving. That is the answer."

Norris wins his first grand prix of year in Hungary

Complete weekend for Norris but poor result for Sainz - driver ratings

Hungarian GP Review: Brilliant Budapest

Norris believes he is driving better this season than he did in the first half of his championship year in 2025.

Last year, he was struggling for feeling from the McLaren.

Like all his rivals, he does not like this new generation of cars as much as the last - especially their engines and the need for so much energy management, and the way they have compromised the driving experience.

But he has gelled with them, while Piastri - so strong in the first half of last season - is struggling.

Team principal Andrea Stella says this is a continuation of the trajectory Norris has been on since a lot of self-assessment led to his strong second half of last year, and eventually the title.

"Lando is much more confident. He's much more aware of his tools that he has in his driving, how to deploy these tools. And I think he's also, let me say, 

"Because today, when he was behind Oscar, he said a couple of times that he had pace in hand, but he didn't get overly frustrated. And the fact that he wasn't overly frustrated, I think, then allowed him to use the pace at the right time and lead him to the victory. We've seen a great trajectory of development for Lando."

This performance came after a major upgrade to the McLaren car, and there is another to come at the next race, the Dutch Grand Prix after F1's four-week summer break.

Norris' win moves him up to 98 points behind Antonelli, but he cautioned against expectations of a charge up to the top of the championship of the kind Max Verstappen and Red Bull mounted against him and McLaren last year.

"I'm just happy with today," Norris said. "It doesn't mean if I'm quick here, we're going to be quick everywhere.

"One thing I've learned for sure is just to have no expectations of the future and just to work in the present. I think that's the way we've been doing everything as a team.

"That's why we're back on top today: just working hard on ourselves as individuals and also as a team.

"Of course, I'm optimistic for the future and I think we can win more races, but we have good competition and there are still plenty of races I'm not confident in because the car is not to the standard that it needs to be in certain areas."

During the race, it appeared as if Piastri's anger over the radio might have been partly directed at the off-set strategy that led to Norris passing him for the lead.

In fact, he was instead furious with Sainz.

"The timing of my stop was fine," he said. "We wanted to cover off Hamilton, which was perfectly normal. Without getting crashed into, I would have been ahead of Lando still.

"In the moment, I was incredibly annoyed. In fact, annoyed is not the word I would use, but there was a multitude that I would, with Carlos. And, yeah, then obviously, when Lando came out ahead, I knew I had no pace to go and attack him.

"I knew my chances of winning the race were done from there."

Discussing the collision with Sainz, Piastri added: "I don't really care if he didn't see me. The fact that he didn't and no-one told him, or there was a lack of complete awareness, is unacceptable.

"He's quite critical of others, and others have given him some stick before for being frustrating on track."

He was not at all mollified by a problem with the GPS system that shows teams where all the cars are on track.

Sainz said he had "no idea I was trying to get lapped", he "didn't expect" Piastri to be there, and it was "impossible to avoid it".

For Piastri, it was academic in the end, a gearbox failure sending him into retirement and denying McLaren a one-two.

As for Ferrari, they appeared to have the fastest car in Hungary, but underperformed in qualifying. Then Hamilton, after qualifying second, was dropped to fifth on the grid with a penalty for impeding Piastri.

Norris will have been worried about Charles Leclerc starting alongside him on the front row. But instead of challenging Norris, Leclerc lost out to Piastri, Verstappen and Hamilton.

The seven-time champion got ahead of Verstappen in the first pit stops - only to be overtaken again the next time around, the Dutchman making a brilliant move at Turn One that caught Hamilton napping.

A penalty for pit-lane speeding cost Hamilton a further five seconds, and left him behind Leclerc at the end, the Ferraris finishing fourth and fifth.

Hamilton, who remains second in the championship, 50 points behind Antonelli, said "you can't make these kind of mistakes if you want to challenge for a title".

Vasseur said: "It's difficult to clearly understand the pace, because I think the clean air is key, but first it's not a good Sunday, because when you are one-two on Friday, you expect much more.

"And on the top we made too many mistakes today, starting with the penalty and the fact that Max overtook us, that each time that we were doing a pit stop, we were losing a position for 0.2 or 0.3 seconds.

"And then we spent our lives behind the guys, everything went wrong, but for sure we have to do a much better job on Sunday."

Norris was followed across the line by Verstappen and Antonelli, both of whom drove fine races themselves, the three podium finishers fully deserving their results.

Antonelli's team-mate George Russell, meanwhile, had another day to forget. A problem with his engine at the start, for which the team took the blame, dropped him to the back at the start, and he recovered well to seventh, but still lost points to the Italian, who he now trails by 59 points.

"I'm sort of past the point of disappointment now, because it's just, if I'm continuing to be disappointed with everything that goes on, I'll just be disappointed every day of the week," Russell said.

"Obviously, another technical issue that completely ruined the race, but I can tell you some positives. The pace was very strong.

"So, I'll take positives there, but yeah, it's just unbelievable, the list of things that's happened this season.

"Oscar had his thing today as well. It's not like we're the only one, but it does feel like it is happening substantially more to me than others, and hopefully it swings around.

"I don't wish any bad luck on anyone, but I've never had a season like this in my whole career, let alone my F1 career."

Antonelli, then, goes off on holiday in total control of the championship. But he knows to take nothing for granted, as this time last year the same looked to be the case for Piastri.

"I think Lando still had the upper hand this weekend, even on us," Antonelli said.

"On pure pace, I don't think I would have been able to challenge him, especially with how difficult it was to follow as well, with a lot of tyre overheating.

"I did not expect to find myself in this position. But the car has been extremely good, the team has done an incredible job and, on my side, I try to maximise every opportunity I have.

"Of course, there's still lots of work to do, lots to learn, but it was a good first half of the season. Now I'm looking forward to the second half and we're just going to keep pushing."

title: Hunter-gatherers introduced fish to a mountain lake 7000 years ago
description: Many centuries before the advent of agriculture in Norway, ancient people transported fish into mountain lakes to create a source of food, then built wooden traps to catch them
fullText:
Hunter-gatherers transported brown trout into the mountains of Norway at least 7000 years ago so they could be harvested during summer foraging trips into the highlands.

That is the only possible explanation for how fish could have populated isolated mountain lakes that had been covered by a kilometres-thick ice sheet for tens of thousands of years, says Axel Mjærum at the University of Oslo, Norway.

“This is the oldest documented example of human-mediated translocation of fish in the world,” says Mjærum.

Until around 8400 years ago, Lake Tesse, at an elevation of around 850 metres, was covered by the Fennoscandian ice sheet, leaving an ecological blank canvas once it retreated.

Yet before it was transformed for hydropower storage in the 1940s, Lake Tesse was regarded as one of the richest brown trout waterways in Norway, yielding 9 tonnes of the fish annually.

While it has long been suspected that humans had a hand in establishing the brown trout population in Lake Tesse, we had no idea how long ago this happened.

Alternative ideas have included transportation by birds or natural migration of fish and eggs upstream. But most Norwegian mountain lakes, including Lake Tesse, only had brown trout until recently, and geographical features such as large waterfalls make natural dispersal upstream impossible.

Mjærum and his colleagues studied the partially buried remains of elaborate wooden fish traps, discovered in 2022 when the lake level was lowered.

Radiocarbon dating showed that the oldest trap dated from around 4950 BC. By correlating the recovered wood with the pine tree ring chronology available for the central Scandinavian mountains, the team was also able to precisely date some of the posts that were part of the younger traps.

One came from a tree felled between spring 2669 BC and winter 2669-2668 BC, and another 12 years later during the winter of 2657-2656 BC, demonstrating that the traps must have been maintained to keep them in good working order.

“Therefore, it is possible that this form of trap fishing was ongoing in Tesse during much of the period between 5000 and 2650 BC,” says Mjærum.

The transport of fish into the lakes is an early example of people managing the environment to provide food, centuries before the advent of farming in Scandinavia. There is evidence that fish farming began even earlier in other parts of the world, including channels and traps for catching eels built in Australia 8600 years ago.

How people transported the fish is unknown, but they may have used waterskins. People probably stayed in the mountains for part of the summer season, hunting reindeer and fishing, but spent the winters in the valleys or along the coast where the climate was milder, says Mjærum.

“A good and predictable food supply also made longer stays possible, not only for hunters aiming for big game, but for whole family groups,” he says.

On Windows use python instead of python3.

Restart Claude Code. That's it — no dependencies, Python 3.8+.

A bare filename matches anywhere in the tree, because that's what you mean

Keep the last three lines. They are what stops the model from disabling its own

exit=2 means it's live. exit=0 on a protected path means the pattern didn't match.

title: Why a Ukrainian cruise missile is flying with hobby drone hardware
description: An open-source flight-control system found in consumer drones has been installed in Ukraine’s latest cruise missile, showing how cheap technology is making military hardware accessible to all
fullText:
Ukraine has developed a cheap cruise missile guided by an open-source autopilot system typically found in consumer drones. The use of hobby components highlights the shrinking gap between military and consumer electronics, which may make it easier for small countries and non-state actors to develop powerful high-tech weapons.

With foreign long-range weapons hard to come by, Ukraine has had to develop its own. Fire Point, a Ukrainian company, showed off its FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile at the Eurosatory defence expo in Paris last month. The 6-tonne missile can carry a warhead twice as heavy as a Tomahawk cruise missile for twice the distance, but costs a fraction as much.

One secret of Flamingo’s low cost is its Ardupilot flight controller, which uses sensor data to keep the missile flying stably along its assigned path.

Ardupilot is an open-source software suite that has been around since 2009, and can run on hardware costing less than $100. Drone hobbyists use Ardupilot on everything from multicopters and model aircraft to boats and ground vehicles.

In a post on X, Fire Point’s Chief Technology Officer Iryna Terekh said open-source software offers independence because it doesn’t come from a company that may go out of business or be blocked from exporting to Ukraine. What’s more, a community of thousands of engineers quickly finds and resolves bugs in the software.

“The use of open-source Ardupilot is in keeping with Fire Point’s whole philosophy of rapidly providing effective long-range strike at a vastly lower cost than exquisite Western designs,” says Roy Gardiner at the non-profit group Defense Tech for Ukraine.

Gardiner notes that Ardupilot is one the world’s most extensively tested autopilots. Ukraine’s vast fleet of small drones, many derived from hobby designs, runs largely on open-source flight controllers such as Betaflight, Ardupilot and PX4.

Russia is also relying heavily on commercial electronics in its Shahed attack drones, according to Ukrainian drone expert Serhii Beskrestnov. Waves of Shaheds hit Ukraine every night, and while earlier versions navigated by satellite, a new “Seeker” version has a camera and Raspberry Pi 4 processor with AI software to lock on to targets, Beskrestnov said on Telegram. The Raspberry Pi, made in the UK, is used in educational and hobby computing projects.

The software on the Shahed hasn’t been identified, but smaller drones often use Raspberry Pi with open-source vision software called YOLO for locking on to targets.

Ukraine has also deployed the more conventional Storm Shadow cruise missiles developed by French and British companies, while Russia has its own high-end Kalibr cruise missiles.

But given the rapid improvement in commercial hardware and open-source software in recent decades, it is unclear how well these legacy systems, with their high costs but arguably superior performance, can compete in the long run. “Over time, expensive custom military electronics and software will likely be developed only for the most demanding requirements,” says Gardiner.

Now, small countries can produce weapons almost as capable as those of their large, well-funded neighbours, and non-state actors can make their own cruise missiles. “The dramatic reduction in cost gives many state and non-state actors access to strike capabilities that were previously available only to the wealthiest nations,” says Gardiner.

title: George Martin never out-wrote the Beatles. That’s exactly why he’s the AI leadership lesson we need now
description: The "Fifth Beatle" didn't have better answers than Lennon and McCartney, the "Dean of Innovation" writes for Fortune—he heard possibilities they couldn't.
fullText:
In 1965, Paul McCartney played George Martin a new song called "Yesterday" and asked what it needed. Martin heard something McCartney hadn't: a string quartet, on a Beatles rock record, when nothing like that had been tried before. McCartney resisted. Martin pushed. The result became one of the most recorded songs in history. That's the story worth remembering as executives rush to put AI in every meeting: the most valuable person in the room isn't always the one with the most answers. Sometimes it's the one who hears a possibility no one else can.

What are the three levels of AI leadership?

What distinguishes judgment from intelligence in leadership?

How should organizations approach AI transformation strategically?

Why is the Age of Answers over?

Today, I tell people something that sounds almost absurd: the Age of Answers is over. Not because answers no longer matter. Quite the opposite. We have more answers than at any point in human history. Artificial intelligence can write business plans, diagnose diseases, analyze markets, draft legal briefs, build software, and produce strategic recommendations in seconds. What once required teams of highly trained experts is rapidly becoming available to anyone with a laptop.

That's precisely the point. When answers become abundant, they stop being a competitive advantage. George Martin proved this decades before AI existed. He wasn't a better songwriter than Lennon or McCartney, nor a better musician than Harrison or Starr. What he brought was a different way of hearing possibility — orchestration, tape experimentation, the willingness to tell four young musicians hard truths about their own material. That is the promise of AI: not a replacement for human creativity, but an amplifier of it, if leaders know how to use it that way.

Compare that to how most organizations use AI today. Within minutes, whiteboards fill with timelines, milestones, decision trees, and Gantt charts. Every team finds the "X" on the map; every team builds the fastest route to get there. Not one team questions whether they're using the right map.

Their thinking is disciplined, their analysis is rigorous, their execution is flawless. There's only one problem: innovation rarely begins with an X on the map. It begins by questioning whether the map describes the right territory in the first place.

For years, helping accomplished leaders make that shift was extraordinarily difficult. Success rewards certainty, while organizations reward predictability. Yet every meaningful breakthrough begins with an uncomfortable admission: What if we're solving the wrong problem?

Today, leaders no longer need to debate the issue. They can simply ask AI to generate the solution they were about to build — usually in less than a minute. That changes the conversation completely. The question is no longer whether AI can produce better answers, but what leaders must do when everyone has access to the same ones.

title: Cities conserve as Colorado River reservoir faces 'dead pool' crisis
description: Phoenix, Tucson, San Diego and Albuquerque conserving water amid looming crisis on the Colorado River.
fullText:
Cities across the Southwest are stepping up conservation efforts amid the growing crisis facing a key Colorado River reservoir straddling the Utah-Arizona border.

While water costs could rise for Southwest residents, according to experts, it is unlikely that changes in the Colorado River will disrupt the availability of drinking water. Still, cities in Arizona, California and New Mexico aren't taking any chances. Some are recycling wastewater and limiting when people can water their lawns, while others are desalinating ocean water.

Their efforts come as Lake Powell – a reservoir that produces power for millions of homes across the West ‒ is the emptiest it has ever been this late in the summer. Its water volume has dropped as long-term climate change creates a warmer and drier West.

Lake Powell was 23.4% full on July 19. It was last full in 1983. If its level falls more, that could create environmental catastrophe by stopping the river flowing through the Grand Canyon, a situation known as "dead pool."

The crisis could create ripple effects nationwide. Nearly half of the country's vegetables and more than three-quarters of its fruits and nuts are grown in California, according to the state's Food and Agriculture Department. A substantial amount of California crops are irrigated with Colorado River water.

Meanwhile, California and the six other states that collaboratively manage the river have been unable to reach a compromise on what to do about the problem.

"At the end of the day, cities have the responsibility to ensure reliable, safe tap water supplies," said Kathryn Sorensen, research director for Arizona State University's Kyl Center for Water Policy. "That's not the responsibility of the state. It's not the responsibility of the federal government. And so you see cities really stepping up."

More: See how Colorado River's shrinking supply is being felt at Lake Powell

Some states have been more impacted than others: Farmers and rural towns in Utah are dealing with "unprecedented" water shortages. Most of the water diverted from the Colorado River is used for farming, while 20% is designated for residential purposes.

Sorensen applauded cities for their conservation efforts but cautioned that much more needs to be done by the biggest water users: farmers.

"We can't solve this problem without the participation of agriculture," Sorensen said. "The scale is too big to solve it on the backs of cities alone."

More: Can desalinization plants solve the west's water problem? | The Excerpt

Cities and states could conserve more water by encouraging better landscaping practices and the installation of low-flow showers and toilets, according to Dave Owen, an associate dean for research at the University of California College of Law in San Francisco.

"The reality is there probably is enough water in the Colorado River to go around, if we are smart about how we use that water," said Owen, who studies water law and environmental policy.

To understand how they are adapting, USA TODAY spoke to government officials and water policy experts in Phoenix, Tucson, San Diego and Albuquerque, cities that all receive significant amounts of water from the Colorado River.

Phoenix has invested in three water purification facilities, has installed leak sensors at city-owned housing and uses technology that controls irrigation schedules based on weather data. The city, which serves 1.7 million water customers, receives about 47.9 million gallons of water annually from the Colorado River.

"We know that conservation can be incredibly meaningful," Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego said.

"We would love to see a collaborative agreement where all users on the river reduce their use," Gallego said. "The cuts would be much more tolerable if everyone were to come to the table, and we'd like to see the national government understand that from national defense to semiconductors, Central Arizona makes an unusually important contribution, and that needs to be something we consider."

Throughout the late 1900s, Tucson replaced many grass lawns with Sonoran desert landscaping, which includes natural rock formations and native plants that require less water.

Over the past 25 years, these efforts have allowed Tucson to fill a reservoir of water from the Colorado River. Despite substantial population growth, the city uses the same amount of water as it did in the late 1980s, according to Director of Tucson Water John Kmiec.

"We have more than six years of ... banking on the ground in the Tucson area that are ready to help buffer any changes or any shortages that may be put on our contract, while they're trying to work out an agreement on the river," Kmiec said.

For San Diego, which has low yearly rainfall averages, the Colorado River is critical. The city receives about 97.8 million gallons of water from the river, according to Meena Westford, who oversees imported water for the San Diego County Water Authority.

San Diego is also home to the country's largest desalination plant, which can supply water to up to 400,000 households annually.

On July 14, the federal government struck an agreement with the Metropolitan Water District of Southern California to pay it up to $65 million to stop drawing water from the Colorado River.

The district, which includes San Diego, also has paid farmers to conserve water and leave parts of their land unplanted.

"Conservation is a way of life in San Diego County," Westford said, "and definitely these new water reuse projects that are coming online should help us manage through some of that drought."

In a drought year, about 70% of Albuquerque's water comes from the Colorado River, according to David Morris, a spokesperson from the Albuquerque Bernalillo County Water Utility Authority.

Albuquerque encourages people to limit watering their plants to three days a week and prohibits watering lawns between 11 a.m. and 7 p.m. Such efforts have helped the city reduce its daily water use from 250 gallons per person in the mid-1990s to about 125 gallons today.

The city has a 100-year water plan dubbed "Water 2120," which considers different scenarios based on climate change and water shortages. Meanwhile, city officials hope to invest 

"We feel like our conservation efforts are succeeding, but we don't feel like they're done yet," Morris said. "We still have a ways to go."

title: Democrats favored to win House, underdogs in Senate 100 days out
description: Democrats are favored to win the House but are slight underdogs in the fight for the Senate with 100 days to go before the midterms, according to the latest forecast from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Both...
fullText:
Democrats are favored to win the House but are slight underdogs in the fight for the Senate with 100 days to go before the midterms, according to the latest forecast from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Both parties are dealing with headwinds as they head into the home stretch of the high-stakes election.

Republicans are worried about the escalation of the Iran war, which only a few weeks ago seemed on the edge of ending. The new fighting risks widening the war as the Iran-backed Houthis move to close the Red Sea to ships. It's all led to a new spike in oil prices, adding to the Trump administration's economic woes.

Democrats, meanwhile, are dealing with a bitter debate about the direction of the party that has given a new line of attack for the GOP.

Wins by democratic socialist and antiestablishment candidates in House primaries across the country have sparked concerns from centrists that their party will be characterized as too extreme. It's a line of attack being emphasized by President Trump and GOP leaders in Washington working to convince voters not to hand power to the Democratic Party.

The result is a situation 100 days out that gives both parties reasons to be hopeful and worried.

"It's a competitive situation in both the Senate and the House," said Geoffrey Skelley, DDHQ's chief elections analyst.

Democrats like their chances in the House, where the GOP is gripping a narrow lead in a midterm year in which the president's party has historically lost seats. In the Senate, Democrats have a shot at the majority but will need to win seats in several states won by Trump.

DDHQ forecasts Democrats winning a 15-seat advantage in a 225-210 House, while Republicans narrowly retain power in a 50-50 Senate with Vice President Vance as the tiebreaker vote. As of late July, Democrats had a 60 percent probability of winning the lower chamber, while Republicans had a 60 percent chance of holding the Senate.

That represents a tightening in the fight for the House since the start of the month, when the model indicated Democrats could have as much as a 25-seat advantage.

And a slight narrowing of the high-stakes cycle is borne out in recent polling on a generic congressional ballot.

DDHQ's averages show Democrats with a 4-point advantage over Republicans on a generic ballot. That includes July polling from YouGov/The Economist, which found Democrats up 5 points in its latest survey, and from Morning Consult, which put Democrats up just 3 points. Last month, the average was closer to a 6- or 7-point edge for Democrats.

A new survey from Emerson College Polling painted a more promising picture for Democrats. It showed them with an 11-point advantage over Republicans on a generic congressional ballot. But it remains to be seen whether that double-digit edge is a sign of momentum or an outlier.

Skelley said the Emerson data "suggests a real range of opinions about what things are going to look like in the fall."

Democrats hope they can capture voters souring on Trump and frustrated with a GOP-controlled Congress.

Voter unhappiness with the economy is driving Trump's lackluster approval numbers. It promises to be the biggest issue of the 2026 midterms and is deeply intertwined with the Iran war.

"The big question is: will the Iranian conflict … will people being concerned about that ratcheting up, is that going to create reverberations in things like the generic ballot that signal 'OK, Democrats' advantage is growing again'?" Skelley said.

On the generic ballot averages, the Democrats' lead expanded as the Iran conflict picked up earlier this year, spiking gas prices in an electoral environment already wrought by economic strain. As the conflict eased somewhat and gas prices fell in the spring, Republicans narrowed the gap in some polling.

"The challenge for Republicans is the Iranian conflict is heating up again," Skelley said, pointing to this past week's news that gas prices were on the rise as the conflict continued to build.

"This is politically very bad for the GOP. For them to try to make a case that Democrats are too extreme, it's a lot easier to make that case if economic conditions are at least OK," he said.

Polling from The Economist/YouGov earlier this month underscored the war's unpopularity, with 57 percent calling the war the wrong decision. Although nearly 8 in 10 MAGA Republicans approved of the war, just 51 percent of non-MAGA Republicans, which represented roughly a quarter of GOP respondents, said the same.

Republican lawmakers have also expressed worry that Trump, who has called affordability concerns a Democratic "hoax," is out of sync with the base on the economy.

"Given that President Trump was elected in part on the strength of how people viewed his handling of the economy during his first term … for polling to show sizable majorities disapproving of his handling of the economy or inflation or other things like that, it's just very bad," Skelley said.

The good news for Republicans is that Democrats also have problems.

Democrats, bruised by 2024 losses and searching for a new standard-bearer ahead of the 2028 presidential race, are divided about the best path forward for the party in a cycle without Trump at the top of the ballot.

Candidates aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) have made headlines with wins in key races this cycle, and insurgent progressives have ousted some longtime incumbents in what many see as a surge of energy within the Democratic base.

Trump has blasted the democratic socialist movement as "communism" and "the biggest threat to our nation there is."

Republicans "are going to be, from here until the fall, trying to sort of blanket the opposition with terms like 'communists' and 'socialists,'" Skelley said.

There's a key test of voter appetite for progressive candidates next month in Michigan, where centrist Rep. Haley Stevens (D) and progressive Abdul El-Sayed are in a competitive Democratic primary to take on presumptive GOP nominee Rep. Mike Rogers in a race that Cook Political Report considers a "toss up" and DDHQ thinks leans toward Democrats.

If El-Sayed emerges from the Aug. 4 primary, though, some Democrats fear that could give Republicans a leg up in the general.

And if Republicans win Michigan in November, they jump to an 86 percent chance of holding the Senate, according to DDHQ.

"If Democrats are going to find a path to a majority, they cannot afford to lose Michigan," Skelley said.

Altogether, the latest polls and forecasts show it's "far from a blue wave kind of environment," he added even as Democrats appear in position to gain ground on Capitol Hill this fall.

At this point in the 2018 cycle, when Democrats won big in the so-called blue wave, the generic ballot showed Democrats up by an average of 7 points or 8 points, DDHQ said, which is double the current edge.

With just more than three months until Election Day, the tight forecasts make races like the Michigan Senate fight must-wins for both parties, adding urgency to the handful of toss-up contests that could decide control on Capitol Hill.

title: Man accused of illegally 'wrestling' protected sharks in Washington state after months-long investigation
description: Body camera video shows a wildlife officer confronting fisherman after months of surveillance over alleged illegal shark catches in Puget Sound.
fullText:
An Oregon man is facing charges for allegedly illegally catching and "wrestling" protected bluntnose sixgill and broadnose sevengill sharks in Puget Sound.

The Washington state Department of Fish and Wildlife recently shared body camera footage of an officer confronting Connor Seifert, 27, in June in Pierce County, Washington.

"You know your shark rules," the officer could be heard on the video telling Seifert. "You can't fully or partially remove sixgill from the water.

Shark Sightings Spike Near America's Beaches As July 4 Crowds Head To Shore For Weekend

"When you wrestle a sixgill to shore like that, you hop on its back, you expose its gills to the air," the officer continued. "You know as well as anybody else does that Puget Sound is a nursery for these sharks. There has been a direct correlation between catching these sharks in this stage in their lives and the mortality of the pups inside the moms."

He added, "Once they exhaust themselves being fought to shore, then all of their babies die. And then, sooner than you know it, you're not going to have sixgill and sevengill returning to Puget Sound anymore."

This came after months of following Seifert's movements and his online posts, with officers finally setting up surveillance so they could catch him making an illegal catch.

Suspect In Viral Monk Seal Harassment Video Says He Was Doxxed As Federal Court Fight Begins

He has been charged in Pierce County with nine counts of unlawful recreational fishing in the second degree and one count of making a false or misleading statement to a public servant. The first is a misdemeanor and the second is a gross misdemeanor.

Misdemeanors carry up to a $1,000 fine and 90 days in jail if found guilty and gross demeanors carry up to a $5,000 fine and a year in jail.

"Fishing for sixgill and sevengill sharks is unlawful, and unfortunately, officers are seeing a growing number of online posts showing these sharks targeted and then unlawfully removed from or partially removed from the water," the department said in a post about Seifert's charges.

Massachusetts Homeowners Stunned After Town Warns July 4 Flags Threaten Endangered Birds

Seifert claimed that he hadn't been targeting the sharks and that he had accidentally caught them, but videos he posted to social media that allegedly showed him holding a shark's mouth open, while sitting on its back and holding it by its tail on the shore while it attempted to get away paint another picture.

The department said it has gotten 14 complaints about Seifert, mainly connected to his allegedly targeting the sharks.

"Puget Sound acts like a nursey for sixgill and sevengill sharks before they head out to the ocean, the department said.

The department added, "This is one of the primary reasons why it is unlawful to target these sharks locally, as the anglers fishing for these creatures are targeting them during a highly volatile era in the animals' lives."

Both shark species are listed as "Species of Greatest Conservation Need" in Washington State.

Bluntnose sixgills are categorized as "near threatened" and broadnose sevengills are "vulnerable," according to the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

A top Democratic socialist leader on Sunday embraced abolishing the Senate, national borders, prisons and more, laying bare the movement's sweeping agenda as ideological divisions within the Democratic Party continue to deepen.

Speaking to Fox News' Shannon Bream, Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) national co-chair Megan Romer fired off a series of "yes" and "true" responses when asked whether the organization's platform calls for dismantling major American institutions.

"[You're advocating for] abolish[ing] the Senate?" Bream asked.

Bill Maher Admits He Could Vote For Jd Vance, Warns 'Cowardly' Democrats Face Socialist Takeover

Romer also affirmed the organization's support for replacing the presidency and Supreme Court, abolishing ICE, eventually eliminating national borders while granting amnesty to people living in the country illegally, defunding the Pentagon, phasing out prisons and shifting most large corporations to public ownership.

She said some proposals, including abolishing borders and prisons, are part of the organization's long-term vision.

Dem Rep Henry Cuellar Rejects Dsa Agenda, Says Socialists Are Trying To 'Use' Democratic Party

Explaining the push to eliminate the Senate, Romer called the chamber "an anachronistic institution" that was designed to limit the influence of ordinary Americans.

"It comes from the British House of Lords," she said.

"The Senate was part of the system that was made to make sure that the people didn't have too much of a say. So we want to expand Congress significantly, but make it a unicameral legislature," Romer said.

Romer also defended the DSA's decision to field candidates on the Democratic ballot line despite criticism from party leaders who argue the organization should build its own political party.

"The two parties have, over years and decades, created a system where ballot line access is extremely difficult for third parties," Romer said.

"We run on the Democratic ballot line where it makes sense. We run independents sometimes where that is a viable possibility, but it's a ballot line. What matters is what the voters think, and the voters are overwhelmingly choosing our candidates," she said.

The comments come as a growing number of prominent Democrats warn the party risks alienating voters by embracing positions championed by the Democratic Socialists of America.

Trump's SAVE America Act stalls as McConnell's absence complicates Senate path
description: Sen. Mitch McConnell's extended Senate absence complicates the SAVE America Act's path through budget reconciliation as Republicans scramble for votes.
fullText:
One key Republican's extended absence and unclear timetable for return is slowing down several legislative priorities, and could impact President Donald Trump's Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) America Act in an unexpected way.

And while sparse statements from Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and his office say he's on the mend, there has yet to be a hard date for when he'll come back to Congress.

It comes as Republicans are twisting and contorting Trump's top election priority into something that could pass the Senate. Though McConnell has voted against the bill before, he would be a key player in crafting what it would look like in the upper chamber.

Trump's Voter Id Bill Catches Unlikely Break As Mcconnell Remains Sidelined

"That could be an issue," Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., told Fox News Digital. "I think there are a lot of issues."

That's because McConnell is chair of the Senate Rules Committee, which will likely be responsible for drafting the version of the SAVE America Act that could pass muster in budget reconciliation, the process that Trump is pushing the GOP to use to pass the bill.

The uncertainty around McConnell, coupled with the late Sen. Lindsey Graham's recent death, throws a wrench into the process. Graham was chair of the Senate Budget Committee, and acted as quarterback through two dances with reconciliation over the past year.

Senate Returns To Packed Agenda After Graham's Death Shrinks Gop Margin

But Graham's replacement on the panel, Johnson, could step in and draft language for SAVE America as chair of the Budget Committee — Graham leapfrogged Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chair Rand Paul, R-Ky., in 2025 to draft his portion of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

"That's my understanding — it actually falls to budget," Johnson said. "So, again… this is still really early in the process, so I don't have all the answers by a long stretch. Plus, we've got to find out what the conference wants to do, and what Leader John Thune wants to do."

Senate Majority Leader Thune, R-S.D., is focusing on preventing a government shutdown, and is encouraging ongoing bipartisan negotiations on a funding deal to continue. And he has threatened to press pause on reconciliation by holding the House's own budget framework until that objective is accomplished.

Gop Rift Grows As Thune Hits Brakes On Trump's Election Bill To Avert Shutdown

He reiterated to Fox News Digital that Republicans don't have the votes to pass the SAVE America Act, and may not have the votes to pass a budget resolution in the upper chamber.

And he noted that the SAVE America Act would have to comply with the Senate's strict rules for reconciliation that unlock the 50-vote threshold, which the current version of the bill does not.

Getting the legislation to a point where it wouldn't slam into those guardrails has remained an open and difficult question for Republicans — Thune suggested that it could work if it's "very carefully structured based upon incentive, mostly grant money," for states.

"So, you know, we're gonna do everything we can to move that forward," Thune said. "But as I told you before, the math on that hasn't changed yet. It's still likely to be a 60-vote exercise, even if it's done with a budget resolution."

Trump demanded Republicans ram through their own budget resolution before they leave Washington, D.C., until after Labor Day on Truth Social Friday to fund defense, agriculture and pass "as much of the SAVE AMERICA ACT as possible."

"Our voters will be extremely happy — And even impressed," Trump said.

Meanwhile, Thune has received criticism from Republicans for his plan to hold up the reconciliation process in favor of averting a shutdown.

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told Fox News Digital the only option to pass SAVE America was through reconciliation, and he's been working on his own plan in the background, and believes it could survive the Senate's "Byrd" test.

"I can't guarantee it, but it's a — I consider it to be a credible argument," Kennedy said. "And I will try to do that, and I will try to, at the right time, bring my colleagues, and, more importantly, the parliamentarian, along. But if we don't do it through reconciliation, through the House reconciliation, we won't get it done."

"And I'm not sure it will work, but I think it might," he continued. "It's at least a 50/50 shot."

title: This red state is strengthening its grip as America's next economic heavyweight
description: IRS migration data reveal over $5 billion in wealth flowing into Texas as Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston and Austin fuel the state's population boom.
fullText:
The race to become America's next economic heavyweight may already have a frontrunner.

The latest Internal Revenue Service (IRS) migration data show billions of dollars in taxpayer wealth flowing into Texas, while Census figures show the state's largest metropolitan areas continue to outpace much of the country in population growth, strengthening a decades-long shift in America's economic center of gravity.

What's more, Texas isn't relying on a single boomtown. Dallas-Fort Worth added more residents than any metropolitan area in the country over the past year, while Houston, Austin and San Antonio also ranked among the nation's fastest-growing metros.

That unusual breadth gives Texas multiple engines of economic growth, providing businesses with larger labor pools, diversified industries and a broader customer base than states anchored by a single dominant city.

Billions In Taxpayer Income Are Leaving Two Iconic States — As A New Economic Map Emerges

The population boom has been accompanied by an influx of wealth. IRS migration data analyzed by the Tax Foundation show the Lone Star State gained more than $5 billion in adjusted gross income from interstate movers, while California and New York recorded multibillion-dollar losses.

"Capital follows where there is confidence," Texas Association of Business Chief Policy Officer Gabriela von zur Muehlen previously told Fox News Digital. "And right now there is a tremendous amount of confidence in Texas."

Von zur Muehlen said Texas' tax structure and predictable regulatory environment continue to attract businesses and investment from other states, helping reinforce the state's economic momentum.

While Florida attracted the nation's largest influx of taxpayer wealth and South Carolina posted the strongest inbound migration rate, Texas stood out by combining billions in new taxable income with rapid growth across Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, Austin and San Antonio.

Economists say that combination matters because higher-income households bring spending, investment, entrepreneurship and tax revenue that can accelerate job creation, fuel commercial development and attract even more businesses. Over time, those forces can transform fast-growing metros into some of the nation's most influential economic hubs.

One Southern City You've Never Heard Of Is Growing Faster Than Anywhere Else In America

Unlike simple population counts, adjusted gross income offers a glimpse into the economic resources newcomers bring with them. Higher-income households can contribute disproportionately to consumer spending, investment and local tax collections, making income migration an important measure of a region's long-term economic strength.

title: Netanyahu accuses Mamdani of 'fomenting hate,' says rhetoric is making New York Jews afraid
description: Benjamin Netanyahu says he still plans to visit New York City for the United Nations General Assembly despite Zohran Mamdani's calls for his arrest under the ICC warrant.
fullText:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani of "fomenting hate," arguing Sunday the democratic socialist's anti-Israel rhetoric is dividing New Yorkers and making the city's Jewish community feel unsafe.

"Look what he's doing. He's fomenting hate. He's supposed to be the mayor of all New Yorkers, Jews, Christians, Muslims, everyone, but he's trying to turn one group against the other," Netanyahu told "Sunday Morning Futures" host Maria Bartiromo.

Netanyahu said Jewish Americans in New York have told him they are growing more fearful.

Jewish Leaders Fault Mamdani Rhetoric As Upper West Side Stabbing, Hate Crime Probe Continues

"They're afraid right now, and I don't think it's accidental that after [Mamdani] made this hate speech against Israel and against me, the next day, a Jew is stabbed coming out of a synagogue," he said.

The Israeli leader was referring to last week's stabbing outside a Manhattan synagogue, where authorities allege 51-year-old Raul Morales stabbed a Jewish man in the chest with a screwdriver while shouting "Allahu Akbar."

Reports also allege Morales yelled the same phrase during a separate stabbing of a 57-year-old Asian man.

Suspect Arrested After Allegedly Yelling 'Allahu Akbar,' Stabbing 2 Men In Nyc Attack

"I think that it's shameful. This thing is very bad for New York. I think it's very bad for peace," Netanyahu said, criticizing Mamdani's rhetoric.

Netanyahu appeared to be referring to Mamdani's remarks from last week, in which Mamdani acknowledged that New York City officials lack the legal authority to arrest Netanyahu under the International Criminal Court's (ICC) warrant, but urged federal officials to do so.

Mamdani called Netanyahu a "war criminal" and "the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people" during the address.

Mamdani Dodges On 'Political Theater' Of Empty Netanyahu Arrest Threat, Calls For Us Action And Nyc Protests

Despite Mamdani's repeated insistence that the Israeli leader is not welcome in New York, Netanyahu said he still intends to travel to the city for the United Nations General Assembly which begins in September, where he vowed to "speak the truth" and defend Israel and its ties to the United States from the podium.

"I'm not concerned [about Mamdani]," Netanyahu said.

"I've appeared just about every year... in my prime ministership, unless there are security conditions, but barring that — and I don't expect that to be the case this time — yes, I do intend to come to New York," he said.

The New York City mayor's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) on Sunday said he does not "expect to get much out of" Dr. Anthony Fauci, former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), during his upcoming Senate hearing.

"I think it'd be very forgetful, completely unrepentant, arrogant, I mean –– arrogant to the extreme," Johnson told Maria Bartiromo on Fox News's "Sunday Morning Futures" when asked about what to expect from Fauci's Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee testimony this week.

"Don't expect to get much out of him, but I'm going to try and lay out all the things that he did that were such a miserably failed response to COVID," Johnson added before the interview ended.

The committee's chair, Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), said Fauci was subpoenaed to testify about an alleged cover-up of the U.S.'s involvement in viral research at a Chinese lab where Paul and other Republicans say the virus that caused the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic was created.

Paul has claimed, without substantial evidence, that the virus was developed in the Wuhan Institute of Virology and somehow escaped as an artificially enhanced virus. He has pointed to Fauci and other health officials as plotting to promote the "lab-leak theory" as a conspiracy theory.

The Kentucky Republican, who blames Fauci for the millions of global COVID-19 deaths, previously told Fox Business that he expects Fauci "will not tell the truth." The two have clashed during past testimonies over COVID-19 while Fauci served as the Biden administration's response to the virus.

"I don't expect him to be honest, he hasn't been honest in the last six years," he said.

Fauci is scheduled to testify on Wednesday.

Former President Biden preemptively pardoned Fauci before leaving office, over concerns the Trump administration would target him. Fauci retired from government work in 2022, having acted as an adviser to presidents since former President Reagan.

Fauci told Paul during a 2021 hearing that the NIAID did not fund gain-of-function research on COVID-19 in the Wuhan Institute of Virology.

Paul said Fauci should be indicted after he claimed the physician lied under oath.

"We've been negotiating with him for material and for testimony," Paul told CNBC last month. "This has gone on for some time. He slow-walked us and slow-walked us. Finally agreed to come in voluntarily … then last week he says he's not coming in. With this subpoena power, we will bring him in, unless he fights this in court."
